summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the dependency adjudication of a child certified as a near fatality, holding the trial court did not abuse its discretion where medical evidence established extensive inflicted injuries and the mother failed to seek treatment.
key_cases.relevance: A hospital child-abuse team's findings supplied the report and the proof supporting intervention.
key_cases.quote: In order to adjudicate a child dependent, the court must determine that the above definition has been met by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: Heinrich v. Conemaugh Valley Memorial Hospital
key_cases.holding: Affirming dismissal on preliminary objections, the court held that hospital staff and physicians who reported suspected child abuse were immune under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6318 because general averments of malice failed to plead the specific facts needed to rebut the statutory presumption of a reporter's good faith.
key_cases.relevance: The published Pennsylvania authority on a mandated reporter's own exposure: § 6318 immunity attaches to the act of reporting and the presumption of good faith must be rebutted with specific facts.
key_cases.quote: We cannot fault Appellees, given the criminal penalty imposed for failing to report suspected child abuse, from making a report under these circumstances.

key_cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment and remanding, the court held that although the CPSL creates no private cause of action for failure to report suspected child abuse, a child may pursue an ordinary medical-malpractice claim where expert testimony would let a jury find that the physicians' standard of care required them to recognize and report the abuse.
key_cases.relevance: The leading Pennsylvania decision on the consequences of not reporting: no CPSL cause of action, but the reporting obligation can form part of a professional's common-law standard of care.
key_cases.quote: the CPSL does not expressly preclude civil liability for a failure to report abuse, nor immunize those who fail in their reporting obligations

state_agency.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth, and Families

mandatory_reporters: Persons licensed or certified to practice in any health-related field under the jurisdiction of the Department of State (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(1))
Medical examiners, coroners and funeral directors (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(2))
Employees of a health care facility or provider licensed by the Department of Health who are engaged in the admission, examination, care or treatment of individuals (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(3))
Employees of a child-care service who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(5))

Clergymen, priests, rabbis, ministers, Christian Science practitioners, religious healers or spiritual leaders of any regularly established church or other religious organization (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(6))

Individuals, paid or unpaid, who on the basis of their role as an integral part of a regularly scheduled program, activity or service are responsible for the child's welfare or have direct contact with children (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(7))
Employees of a social services agency who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(8))
Peace officers and law enforcement officials (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(9))
Emergency medical services providers certified by the Department of Health (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(10))
Employees of a public library who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(11))
Individuals supervised or managed by a person listed under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(1) through (11) or (13) who have direct contact with children in the course of employment (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(12))

Attorneys affiliated with an agency, institution, organization or other entity, including a school or regularly established religious organization, that is responsible for the care, supervision, guidance or control of children (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(14))

Adult family members who are responsible for the child's welfare and provide services to a child in a family living home, community home for individuals with an intellectual disability or host home for children which are subject to supervision or licensure by the department under Articles IX and X of the Public Welfare Code (23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a)(16))
reporting_details: Pennsylvania is not a universal-reporting state: only the categories of mandated reporters listed in 23 Pa.C.S. § 6311(a) are required to report, and they must report immediately to ChildLine (1-800-932-0313) or electronically under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6313(a)(1) with a written report within 48 hours, while any other person may report to the department, the county agency or law enforcement under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6312.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately if emergency protective custody is or may be required; otherwise see the child within 24 hours
timeline_requirements.starts_from: County agency receives the report from the Department of Human Services (ChildLine)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No consequence stated in 23 Pa.C.S. § 6368(b); county agency performance is reviewable by the department under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days in all cases; reasons for delay must be recorded if not completed within 30 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation commenced by the county agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The particular reasons for delay past 30 days must be described in the child protective service record and made available to the department to determine whether the county agency strictly followed 23 Pa.C.S. Ch. 63 and whether it is subject to action under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6343
